They will explain how the chapter reveals its plot twist and escalates tension, and they will summarize how these central ideas are resolved, keeping the summary distinct from their own opinions."},{"kind":"language","text":"Students will use context clues and word parts to determine the meaning of ten Tier 2 and Tier 3 words from the chapter. They will use the words accurately in speaking and writing, and they will expand noun phrases with precise adjectives when describing characters and ideas."},{"kind":"foundational-skills","text":"Students will build fluency by reading a passage from Chapter 22 aloud with accuracy, appropriate pacing, and expression that matches the mood of the scene."}],"essentialQuestions":["How do the characters' choices show a modern interpretation of \"home\" and \"destiny,\" compared to traditional myths?"],"connections":{"knowledgeBuilding":"In Chapter 21 (pp. 344–353), students analyzed how Percy, Zeus, and Poseidon respond to the crisis and to one another. Today they see how the novel resolves that conflict and the personal choices that follow it. Percy's choice about where he belongs sets up the comparison with the Odyssey excerpt in tonight's homework.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories often show that identity is shaped by the choices we make, not only by the fate we are born into. Resolutions in a text reveal what the author most wants readers to understand.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 34 students will move to writing and study variations from standard English while finishing Chapter 22 (pp. 370–375). The Odyssey excerpt will let them compare how a traditional myth and a modern novel treat home and destiny.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students must explain how themes are resolved at the end of a text. having a certain attitude or tendency","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"enroll","definition":"to officially sign up to join a school, program, or group","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"devising","definition":"thinking up or planning something carefully, often a clever plan","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"alliances","definition":"agreements or partnerships between people or groups who join together for a shared goal","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"commemorates","definition":"honors and helps people remember an important person or event","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"vacated","definition":"left empty; moved out of a place","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"harpies","definition":"in Greek myth, winged monsters with the faces of women and the bodies of birds","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"celestial","definition":"having to do with the sky or heavens; divine","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"theme","definition":"a message or big idea about life that a story develops","tier":"support"},{"word":"resolution","definition":"the part of a story where the main conflict is settled","tier":"support"},{"word":"destiny","definition":"the future that seems set for a person, as if by fate","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapter 22, pp. 354–363 (student reading); pp. 364–369 (teacher read-aloud)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate their thinking about what \"home\" means and whether people choose who they become or are born to it, so they are ready to track these ideas in the final scenes.","activities":[{"id":"launch-home-destiny-turn-and-talk","title":"Where Do You Belong?","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.2"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with a partner. Take about one minute each to answer the question on the board."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"For the last few lessons, Percy has been heading toward an ending. Today we read the final scenes, where he has to decide where he belongs. Before we read, think about your own idea of home."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Is home a place, a group of people, or a choice you make? Explain your thinking."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think home is the people, not the place. My family moved last year, and our new house feels like home because we are all together. So home is something you make with people you care about."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Do you think a person's future is already decided for them, or do their choices shape it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think it's both. You can be born with some things, like a talent, but what you do with it is your choice."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Hold on to these ideas. In the traditional Greek myths, heroes often follow a destiny set by gods. Today we look at whether Percy's story agrees or does something new."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Students are sharing opinions now. Later in the lesson they will need to separate opinions from a summary of the text, so you can name that contrast: \"These are your ideas. Soon we will write what the text says.\""}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students learn ten Chapter 22 words in context and build fluency by reading a passage aloud.","activities":[{"id":"lab-vocab-in-context","title":"Words in Context: Tradition to Celestial","minutes":6,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6","L.6.5","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Introduce New Words Using Context Clues and Word Parts","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 22","pages":"pp. 354–362 (words appear on pp. 354, 356, 359, 360, 362)"},{"type":"directions","text":"Turn to the page for each word. Read the sentence it is in, plus the sentence before and after. Decide what the word means, then check the definition your teacher gives."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Pages and sentences may vary slightly between editions. Before class, find each word on the page listed in the Outline and have the sentence ready to read aloud. Teach the words in three quick groups so the 6 minutes do not become a list."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Group 1, camp life: *tradition* (p. 354), *procession* (p. 354), *enroll* (p. 356), *commemorates* (p. 359). Read each sentence aloud. Point out word parts: *pro-* means \"forward\" and *cess* comes from a Latin root meaning \"go,\" so a procession is people going forward together. *Com-* means \"together\" and *memor* means \"remember,\" so *commemorates* means \"remember together.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using *pro-* (forward) and the sentence on p. 354, what do you think *procession* means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It's when people walk forward in a line, like at a ceremony or a parade. The sentence says it is part of a camp tradition, so it's something organized."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Group 2, plans and people: *disposed* (p. 356), *devising* (p. 359), *alliances* (p. 359). Say: *Devising* is a thinking word, as in devising a plan. *Alliances* shares a root with *ally*. Notice *disposed* is a multiple-meaning word. We can \"dispose of\" trash, but here it means \"inclined\" or \"willing.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What clue in the sentence helps you pick the right meaning of *disposed*?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The sentence is about how someone feels toward another person, not about throwing something away. So *disposed* has to mean something like \"leaning toward\" or \"willing.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Group 3, the mythic world: *vacated* (p. 360), *harpies* (p. 360), *celestial* (p. 362). *Vacated* has the root *vac*, meaning \"empty,\" as in *vacuum* and *vacant*. *Harpies* are a Greek myth word, so look at how the author uses myth in a modern setting. *Celestial* means \"of the sky or heavens.\""},{"type":"directions","text":"In your Personal Dictionary, write each word, a short definition in your own words, and a clue from the sentence that helped you. Finish at least five words today. Complete the rest for homework."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support multilingual learners in using context clues and word parts to determine word meaning and use the new words in precise noun phrases.","sayAsk":"Say each word chorally, then with a partner. Ask: What clue in the sentence helps you? Frames: I think ___ means ___ because the sentence says ___. The word part ___ means ___. Noun phrase builder: Percy joined a ___ procession. / Percy followed a ___ tradition. Connect to cognates: tradition/tradición, procession/procesión, celestial/celestial, alliances/alianzas, commemorates/conmemora.","watchFor":"If students copy a dictionary definition without understanding, then ask them to draw or act out the word and restate it in their own words. If students use only one word part, then prompt: What does the whole sentence tell you? Success looks like a student naming a context clue and a word part to support a meaning."}]},{"id":"lab-fluency-partner-read","title":"Fluency: Echo and Partner Reading","minutes":4,"standards":["RL.6.10","L.6.6"],"routine":"Echo Reading and Partner Reading","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 22","pages":"p. 354 (first two paragraphs), or a short passage you select from pp. 354–356"},{"type":"directions","text":"Listen as your teacher reads one sentence at a time and echo it back. Then read the passage aloud to your partner, taking turns by paragraph. Partners listen for accuracy, pacing, and expression."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Read with the mood of the scene. This is a ceremony, so notice where your voice should slow down. When you reach an unfamiliar word, use what we just practiced and try again."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words did you read more smoothly the second time? Why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"*Procession* was hard the first time, but after we talked about it I knew how to say it and I could read the whole sentence without stopping."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and listen to three or four pairs. Note students who skip endings or rush through punctuation. A quick \"Read that sentence once more, pausing at the comma\" is enough feedback."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students read pp. 354–363 closely to track home, choice, and identity, hear the climactic scene on pp. 364–369 read aloud to see how the plot twist and rising tension are built, and then write a summary of how the central ideas are resolved that is distinct from opinion.","activities":[{"id":"lia-track-home-choice-identity","title":"Part A: Track Home, Choice, and Identity","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.3"],"routine":"Close Read and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 22","pages":"pp. 354–363"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Authors rarely say a theme outright. They show it through what characters choose, say, and feel. As you read, look for moments where someone chooses between two things, and think about what the choice says about home or identity."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 354–363. Make a three-column chart labeled: **Choice or moment** (with page number), **What it shows about home, choice, or identity**, and **Traditional myth comparison**. Record at least three moments. Quote or paraphrase each, and note the page."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Page-level details differ by edition. As students read, listen for Percy deciding where he will spend the school year and what he says about his mother, for how Percy and his friends talk about the end of summer and returning home, and for any moment where Percy, Annabeth, or Grover decide how much to trust or stay loyal to someone. Redirect students to what is actually on the page. Do not supply details they have not found."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What choice does Percy make in these pages, and what does it show about how he thinks of home?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy chooses to go back home to his mom instead of staying at camp all year. On the page it shows he doesn't think home is only where gods and heroes are. It's where his family is, even if his life there is hard."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In a traditional myth, a hero's fate is often set by the gods. How is Percy's decision different?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the old myths, heroes usually follow what the gods or the prophecy say. Percy has a prophecy too, but he still gets to decide for himself where he belongs. That makes it a more modern idea of destiny."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What evidence from pp. 354–363 shows that Percy's identity has changed since the start of the book?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"At the beginning he was a kid who thought he was a failure. Now the text shows him being trusted by his friends and making his own big decision, so he sees himself as someone who can choose and be brave."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support multilingual learners in reading closely and expanding noun phrases to describe characters and themes with precision.","sayAsk":"Have students first tell a partner what happens in the passage in everyday language, then restate using academic frames. Frames: On page ___, Percy chooses ___, which shows ___. In a traditional myth, ___, but in this story ___. Noun phrase expansion: Percy makes a ___ choice. (difficult / loyal / unexpected) Percy has a ___ idea of home. (modern / personal / family-centered)","watchFor":"If students retell the plot without analysis, then prompt: What does this choice show about the theme? If students leave out the page number, then say: Show me where in the text you found that. Success looks like a student pairing a quoted detail with a sentence explaining what it shows."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Finding a choice that connects to a theme","tryThis":"Give a two-step prompt: What did the character decide? What does that decision say about home or who he is? Let students point to the sentence first and talk before they write."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find a moment where two themes, such as home and identity, appear in the same choice, and to explain how the author connects them. Invite them to find a word choice on pp. 354–363 that carries a strong connotation and explain its effect (RL.6.4)."}]}]},{"id":"lia-read-aloud-climax","title":"Part B: Teacher Read-Aloud of the Climactic Scene","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.3","RL.6.5","RL.6.1","RL.6.4","RL.6.6"],"routine":"Teacher Read-Aloud with Listening Tracker","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 22","pages":"pp. 364–369 (teacher read-aloud)"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Now I will read the climactic scene aloud. Listen like a detective. Mark the moment the plot twist is revealed and the places where the tension goes up. Jot down the words that make you feel it."},{"type":"directions","text":"Listen as your teacher reads pp. 364–369. On your listening tracker, make two columns: **Where the twist is revealed or the tension rises (page and quote)** and **How the author creates that feeling**. Add at least two entries."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Read slowly and use pauses before big reveals. Stop only once, after the main twist, for a 30-second turn and talk. Read the rest straight through so the tension carries. Plan your pauses before class, since page details differ by edition."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What twist does the author reveal in this scene, and how does the plot change after that moment?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The twist is that Luke is the one who has been working against Percy the whole time. After that, the scene gets much more dangerous, because the person Percy trusted becomes the threat."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What specific words or details make the tension build?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The author uses short, fast sentences and shows Luke's anger and bitterness. When Percy realizes he was betrayed, the language gets sharper and the pace speeds up, so I felt nervous."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why do you think the author places this scene at the end of the book? How does it help the theme?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It puts Percy in a spot where he has to choose between anger and loyalty, or between fate and his own decision. That tests what he has learned about family and who he is, so it helps develop the theme."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support multilingual learners in comprehending the read-aloud and evaluating how language choices create tension.","sayAsk":"Pause after the twist and let students turn to a partner. Ask: Which words made the scene feel tense? Frames: The author uses the word ___ to show ___. The tension rises when ___. The twist changes the plot because ___. Give a bank of tension words: betrayal, danger, bitter, shock, trust.","watchFor":"If students cannot follow the fast pace, then re-read one key sentence slowly and show it on a document camera. If students describe feelings only, then prompt: Which word on the page made you feel that? Success looks like a student naming a specific word or detail and explaining its effect."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Tracking tension and the plot twist while listening","tryThis":"Provide a sentence-starter tracker: Before the twist, ___. After the twist, ___. Replay the single key paragraph and let students underline it in their own books."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to describe how the narrator's point of view, with Percy telling the story in first person, shapes what readers learn about the twist and when we learn it (RL.6.6)."}]}]},{"id":"lia-summarize-theme-resolution","title":"Part C: Summarize How the Themes Are Resolved","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.2","RL.6.1","L.6.6","RL.6.5"],"routine":"Quick Write with Pulse Check","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 22","pages":"pp. 354–369"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A summary says what the text shows. It does not say whether you liked it. Compare: an opinion says, \"I think Percy made the right choice.\" A summary says, \"Percy chooses to return home to his mother, which shows that for him home means family and not only the camp.\" Use words like *shows*, *reveals*, and *suggests*, and use at least one vocabulary word."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write a 4–5 sentence summary that explains how the ideas of home, choice, and identity are resolved in Chapter 22. Use at least two pieces of evidence from pp. 354–369, with page numbers, and one vocabulary word from today. Do not include your opinion."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Model for display, if needed: In Chapter 22, the ideas of home, choice, and identity come together as Percy makes his own decisions after the climax. The text shows that after the betrayal is revealed, Percy chooses to go home to his mother rather than accept the path others expect (p. ___). This suggests that home is about family, not only a place. Percy's choices also reveal that he sees himself as more than a hero in a prophecy. Together, these details show that the novel resolves its themes by treating destiny as something a person shapes through choices. Fill in the page numbers from your edition."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which sentence in your summary is evidence, and which sentence explains what the evidence shows?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My second sentence is evidence, because it says Percy chooses to go home on page 358. My third sentence explains it by saying that shows home means family to him."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.2"],"stem":"Which statement is the best summary of how Chapter 22 resolves the themes of home and destiny, without adding an opinion?","choices":[{"text":"Percy should have stayed at camp because it is safer, so the ending is disappointing.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is an opinion about what Percy should have done. A summary reports what the text shows, not a judgment about it."},{"text":"Percy makes his own choice about where he belongs, which shows that home is tied to family and that destiny includes personal decisions.","correct":true,"rationale":"This states a theme from Percy's choices and the text details without adding a personal judgment."},{"text":"The chapter is only about a betrayal and has nothing to say about home or choice.","correct":false,"rationale":"The betrayal is the plot twist, but it is also what pushes Percy to make decisions about loyalty and where he belongs, so this ignores the themes."},{"text":"Percy follows the exact path the gods planned, just like heroes in traditional myths.","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses the traditional-myth pattern with this story. Percy has a prophecy, but the chapter emphasizes his own choices."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support multilingual learners in writing a summary that separates evidence from opinion and uses precise noun phrases and new vocabulary.","sayAsk":"Let students rehearse their summary orally in a partner or home language first. Frames: In Chapter 22, ___ chooses ___. This shows that ___. One theme the author resolves is ___. Replace opinion words (I think, I like) with text words (the text shows, the author reveals). Noun phrase expansion: Percy's decision about home shows a ___ idea of destiny. (personal / modern / hopeful)","watchFor":"If students write opinion statements like I think or it was good, then prompt: Rewrite using The text shows. If students give a detail with no explanation, then prompt: Add a sentence beginning This shows. Success looks like a student separating evidence from explanation and keeping judgment out."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Writing a summary without opinion","tryThis":"Give a fill-in frame: In Chapter 22, Percy chooses ___. The text shows this when ___ (p. ___). This suggests the theme that ___. Let students say each sentence aloud before writing."},{"type":"situation-placeholder-removed","rows":[]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students synthesize the ending and connect today's work to the Performance Task.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-exit-ticket","title":"Exit Ticket: How Is the Theme Resolved?","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.2","L.6.6"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the Performance Task, Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, you will explain how a theme is resolved at the end of a text. Today you practiced that skill with Chapter 22: finding the choices, tracking the twist, and writing a summary that sticks to the text."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the sentences, using at least one vocabulary word: In Chapter 22, the author resolves the idea of ___ by showing ___. A choice that supports this is ___ (p. ___). One word from today that helped me understand the chapter is ___ because ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 22, the author resolves the idea of home by showing that Percy picks his family over the safety of camp. A choice that supports this is Percy deciding to go back to his mom (p. ___). One word from today that helped me is *alliances*, because it helped me understand why the friendships among the characters mattered."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Collect the exit tickets to see who can state a theme tied to a specific choice and page. These students are ready for the comparison with the Odyssey. Students who write only a plot summary should be seen in a small group before Lesson 34."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (optional)","purpose":"Students keep reading and prepare for the comparison to a traditional myth.","activities":[{"id":"homework-ch22-odyssey","title":"Read and Annotate: Chapter 22 (pp. 370–375) and the Odyssey Excerpt","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","L.6.4"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"1) Read and annotate The Lightning Thief, Chapter 22, pp. 370–375. Mark one place where Percy shows what home means to him, and one place where a choice reveals identity. 2) Read and annotate the excerpt from the Odyssey. Mark one detail about how the hero thinks about home or about the role of the gods in his journey. Finish the Personal Dictionary entries for today's ten words if you did not complete them in class."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Tell students the Odyssey excerpt will be compared with Percy's story, so they should notice how Odysseus thinks about home and fate. This prepares them for the traditional-versus-modern comparison."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students read Chapter 22 (pp. 354–363) closely and hear the climactic scene (pp. 364–369) read aloud, tracking how Percy's choices develop the themes of home, choice, and identity and how the plot twist raises tension.
